---
title: "Feature matrix"
subtitle: "What each package does today"
---

Both packages implement the same method: convolution interpolation with the same kernels, the
same boundary conditions and the same derivative and integral operators, so a result computed in
one language is reproducible in the other. ConvolutionInterpolations.jl is the reference
implementation; convinterp is a port with a Rust core, tested against the Julia package to the
last bit of the boundary coefficients. The port is younger, and the rows below say exactly how
far it has come.

| Capability | Julia | Python | Concept page |
|:--|:--:|:--:|:--|
| Interpolation on uniform grids, any dimension | ✓ | ✓ | [Interpolation and kernels](concepts/interpolation.qmd) |
| Kernels `a0`…`a7`, `b5`…`b13` | ✓ | ✓ | [Interpolation and kernels](concepts/interpolation.qmd) |
| Boundary conditions `poly`, `detect`, `linear`, `quadratic` | ✓ | ✓ | [Boundaries](concepts/boundaries.qmd) |
| Extrapolation beyond the data (`throw`, `flat`, `line`, `natural`) | ✓ | — | [Boundaries](concepts/boundaries.qmd) |
| Derivatives, per axis, up to the kernel's range | ✓ | ✓ | [Derivatives](concepts/derivatives.qmd) |
| Integrals, any order, per axis, mixed with derivatives | ✓ | ✓ | [Integrals](concepts/integrals.qmd) |
| Nonuniform grids (`n3`, `b5`…`b13`) | ✓ | — | [Nonuniform grids](concepts/nonuniform.qmd) |
| Per-axis kernels and mixed uniform/nonuniform axes | ✓ | — | [Nonuniform grids](concepts/nonuniform.qmd) |
| Gaussian smoothing (`convolution_smooth`, `convolution_gaussian`) | ✓ | — | [Smoothing](concepts/smoothing.qmd) |
| Grid-to-grid resampling (`convolution_resample`) | ✓ | — | [Interpolation and kernels](concepts/interpolation.qmd) |
| Scattered data, exact and smoothing fits (`fit_scattered`) | ✓ | — | [Scattered data](concepts/scattered.qmd) |
| Adaptive and user-supplied knot grids for scattered data | ✓ | — | [Scattered data](concepts/scattered.qmd) |
| Lazy construction for large grids and high dimensions | ✓ | — | [Interpolation and kernels](concepts/interpolation.qmd) |
| `Float32`, `BigFloat` and other element types | ✓ | — | [Interpolation and kernels](concepts/interpolation.qmd) |
| Zero-allocation evaluation | ✓ | ✓ | [Julia](benchmarks/julia/index.qmd) and [Python](benchmarks/python/index.qmd) benchmarks |
## Reading the matrix

- A ✓ in both columns means the same call with the same arguments gives the same numbers,
  up to floating-point rounding, in both languages; the concept pages show the two side by side.
- A ✓ in the Julia column only means the feature exists in the reference implementation and is
  not yet ported. The concept page documents it with Julia code and says so at the top.
- The port's Rust core evaluates in `f64` only. Extended and reduced precision are a Julia
  feature, since the kernels are stored as exact rationals and the Julia code is written
  generically over the element type.

## What the port will get next

The order follows the Julia package's own history: extrapolation beyond the data, nonuniform
grids, then smoothing and resampling, then scattered data. Each row moves to ✓ in the release
notes of the version that ships it, and this page is updated with the release.
